newsitem.title: JAPAN: Exxon talks could spur further Japan alliances.
newsitem.headline: Exxon talks could spur further Japan alliances.

text.p: Negotiations involving a possible refinery and storage sharing agreement between three Exxon Corp affiliates could result in a flurry of follow-up alliances, oil industry analysts said on Monday.

Japan's Esso Sekiyu, General Sekiyu KK and Tonen Corp are the latest companies to discuss downstream consolidation since Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Showa Shell Sekiyu KK announced plans last February to potentially merge parts of their oil refinery and distribution systems.

Company officials from both Esso Sekiyu and General Sekiyu said they were considering a cooperative agreement involving their operations and Tonen's in the city of Kawasaki that would potentially save the three companies four billion yen.

"Oil firms affiliated to oil majors are very efficient and have already taken drastic steps to restructure their businesses. Therefore, a decision between the three (Exxon affiliates) will force Japanese oil firms (with no ties to majors) to take countermeasures to maintain competitiveness," said Tatsuru Suzuki, a senior economist with the LTCB Research Institute.
"Japanese oil firms will consider the move as a serious threat. It's likely to fuel an industry shake-up," he said.
"Japan's oil refineries have too much refining capacity and with deregulation last year profit margins have been squeezed.
"Oil firms need to slash costs to survive," he said.

Another factor frustrating refiners' efforts to cut costs in the newly liberalised marketplace has been the weak yen, which has kept the cost of importing oil relatively high in spite of the falling crude market in the first quarter of 1997.

"We have seen our crude import costs rising steadily because of the yen's weakness against the dollar, while the prices we received for our refined products have been hit by deregulation," an industry official said.
The yen hit a 56-month low of 127.10 to the dollar in early Tokyo trade and was standing at 126.90 in afternoon trade.

Because refiners make their crude purchases on a dollar per barrel basis, while prices for refined products like gasoline and heating oil are tied to the yen, dollar per barrel refinery profit margins have been negatively affected.
"We are constantly fighting to maintain a $1.50 per barrel simple refining margin," the official added.
